Notes: Earliest documented Jewish presence (basis for Year Established): Italian Ministry of Culture press release (March 2025, quoting Ostia park director Alessandro D'Alessio) cites 'la più antica iscrizione nota in Italia che menzioni Iudaei, rinvenuta nella vicina necropoli di Pianabella', dated to the beginning of the 1st century CE (early 1st c. CE; year c. 25 used as midpoint of 'inizi del I secolo'). The funerary inscription (found by chance 2006 at Pianabella, the necropolis SE of Ostia) names several persons as Iudaei; the release speaks of continuous Jewish presence at Ostia through the imperial period. Suggests a small resident group/families of Judaeans; no count. Caveat: other commentators (B. Nongbri) note the 1st-c. date on the museum label is possible but not certain. No classical or Jewish literary source mentions Jews at Ostia. Population blank: presence only.

Synagogue at Ostia (excavated 1961-62 by M. Floriani Squarciapino): she writes that the 4th-c. synagogue stood on an earlier building 'whose masonry, in opus reticulatum, pointed to a date in the first century A.D.' and concludes 'the Jewish community of Ostia had its own synagogue from the first century A.D. on' (Archaeology 16.3, 1963, pp. 194-203). 1st c. CE = year 50 (midpoint; c.). Indicates an organized, prosperous community with a sizeable communal building; no count. Dating contested: Squarciapino's 1961 report left open whether the 1st-c. building was already a synagogue, and in 1970 she placed it in the second half of the 1st c. CE, after Claudius' harbour; the Ostia park panel says c. mid-1st c.; Runesson (2001) second half of 1st c.; L.M. White (HTR 1997) Trajanic/Hadrianic and originally a private insula; the UT/White excavation team now dates the complex no earlier than the early 3rd c. CE. Population blank.
